chapter 04 · context

The context window is the whole state

An agent has no memory. It has a transcript, re-read from nothing on every single step, and that transcript is the only thing standing between step 1 and step 30. Deciding what goes into it is the central design act of building an agent — and the one most people skip, because the first ten steps work fine without thinking about it.

In your terms: this is feature engineering, moved to run time. You already know the representation decides whether the algorithm can work. Same problem, new substrate — except the features are chosen while the thing is running, by you, in the shape of what your tools return.

01

Context is a working set, not storage

The reframe that makes the rest obvious.

The instinct is to treat a long window as a place to keep things. It is not. It is a bounded working set that you curate, every step, into the smallest high-signal set of tokens that still supports the next decision.

Everything else — the raw matrices, the full QC tables, the thousands of called loops, the trajectory — lives outside, and the agent holds a handle to it. That is the whole discipline, and the four mechanisms below are just ways of applying it.

02

What the evidence actually says about length

Degradation is real. The clean law people quote is not.

You will hear that models degrade past some fraction of their advertised window. The honest version: degradation with length is well evidenced, but it is task-, model- and position-dependent, and there is no universal curve to design against.

FindingWhat it showedWeight
Lost in the Middle
Liu et al., TACL 2024		A U-shaped curve: relevant information in the middle of a long input is used worst. Going from 20 to 50 retrieved documents bought ~1–1.5% despite better retriever recall.peer-reviewed; the canonical positional-bias result
RULER
COLM 2024		17 models at 4k–128k across retrieval, multi-hop tracing, aggregation, QA. Useful for length sweeps.peer-reviewed; a suite aggregate, not a deployment number
"Context rot"
Chroma, 2025		18 models; ~300-token focused prompts beat full ~113k-token histories consistently; degradation with length across families.⚠ vendor technical report, image-only headline scores — strong controlled evidence, not a peer-reviewed law

"Context rot" is a label coined in a 2025 vendor report, not an established scholarly term. The underlying effect is real and separately evidenced by the positional-bias literature — use the phenomenon, and be careful quoting the phrase as if it were settled science. The practical consequence is unaffected either way: a focused prompt beats a long one, so put less in.

03

Four mechanisms

In order of how much they repay the effort.

1 · Shape every tool result before it enters the transcript

By far the highest-leverage, and the one entirely under your control. A tool should return a synopsis, not its output: counts, ranges, QC flags, the top-k rows, and a handle — a path, an ID, a checksum — plus a companion tool that can fetch detail on demand.

# instead of 10 000 rows:
"3142 loops called (chr1–chr22,X). median span 185 kb; 2 QC flags: "
"low cis/trans on chr9, depth dip 44.2–44.9 Mb. "
"full table: run17/loops.bedpe  — use loops_query(region=…) for detail"

Pagination, range selection, filtering and truncation are the standard moves; a production coding agent caps tool results in the tens of thousands of tokens by default. Pick your cap on purpose rather than discovering it.

2 · Keep explicit state outside the window

A structured run ledger — objectives, completed stages, assertions established, artefact handles with checksums, unresolved anomalies, next actions — written to a file the agent can re-read selectively. This is what survives a compaction, a crash, or a fresh session.

Do not let similarity search stand in for provenance. Retrieving a probably relevant note is fine for prose and wrong for a numerical claim or a file identity. If the agent needs to know which genome build produced an artefact, that is a lookup with an exact answer, not a nearest neighbour.

3 · Compact finished phases — and keep the pointers

Summarize completed work, retaining decisions, unresolved problems, and handles; drop redundant tool results. The documented failure is predictable and unavoidable: aggressive compaction discards the subtle fact whose relevance was not yet apparent. Compaction is lossy by construction, so keep the handles — a pointer costs nothing and makes the loss recoverable.

The peer-reviewed version of this is subgoal-scoped: replace a finished subgoal's trace with a summary while keeping full detail for the current one. HiAgent reports roughly a twofold success-rate increase and ~3.8 fewer steps across five long-horizon tasks doing exactly that.

4 · Delegate verbose work to a subagent

A worker explores in its own window and returns a bounded report. The large output never touches the main transcript. Real, documented, and genuinely useful — but it is a whole chapter's worth of trade-offs, and it only works for separable work with an explicit contract.

04

The design question, stated properly

What is in the context at step n — and why each thing earns its place.

This is the chapter's acceptance test, and it is worth writing down literally for any agent you build. Everything in the window should survive the question "what decision does this support?"

InWhy it earns the tokens
the goal, verbatimre-read every step; it is what "on task" means
tool definitionsthe model cannot call what it cannot see
the run ledger (compacted)what has been established and what is still open
last few steps, in fullimmediate cause and effect — the error it is recovering from
synopses + handles for everything olderenough to decide; enough to fetch detail if needed
OutWhy
raw matrices, full tables, trajectorieshandles instead — the agent can fetch what it needs
tool output nobody readit cost tokens and changed no decision
superseded intermediate resultsa stale number in the window is worse than no number
long successful stages, verbatimcompact to the assertion they established

Exercise p3 — measure it, don't assume it. This chapter is the one where you can see the effect rather than take it on faith.

Do thisWhat you should see
Run p1's agent on a task needing ~20 steps, tool output unshapeda run that degrades — repeats itself, loses the goal, or stops making progress
Log tokens-in per stepthe curve that explains it
Add synopsis + handle to the noisiest tool onlymost of the recovery, from one tool
Compact everything older than five steps, keeping handleshow much further the same task now gets
Compact aggressively, dropping handlesthe documented failure, on purpose — it cannot recover the detail

You can now state, for an agent you are building, exactly what enters the context at step n and what is deliberately excluded, with a reason per item — and you have measured a long run failing and repaired it by shaping observations.

Next: handles point at things the agent can fetch. But what if the knowledge it needs was never in the weights and is not in this run either — a corpus of papers, a codebase, a reference? That is chapter 05.
